translation:
  text: 'I say to him, “Sir, ask him whether, since he has been in my house, I have done anything improper
    that offended him.”


    2. “I myself know,” he said, “that you have done nothing improper and will not do so. I speak with
    you about these things so that you may persevere. For this one has given me a good account of you.
    Tell these words to the others, so that those who have repented or will repent may share your understanding,
    and this one may speak well of them to me, and I in turn to the Lord.[a]”


    3. “Sir,” I said, “I tell every person about the Lord’s mighty works. I hope that all who have sinned
    before, if they hear these things, will gladly repent and regain life.”


    4. “Persevere, then, in this service,” he said, “and complete it. Whoever carries out this one’s commandments
    will have life, and he will have great honor before the Lord.[b] But whoever does not keep his commandments
    flees from their own life and acts against him.[c] They do not follow his commandments but hand themselves
    over to death, and each becomes guilty of their own blood. As for you, I tell you to serve these commandments,
    and you will have a remedy for sins.”'
  philosophy: optimal-equivalence
  footnotes:
  - marker: a
    reason: lexical_alternative
    text: 'The final Latin phrase is elliptical: “and I before the Lord.” “Speak well” is carried over
      from the preceding clause; it is not a separately expressed verb. “Interpret favorably” or “give
      a favorable account” are alternatives for bene interpretetur.'
  - marker: b
    reason: lexical_alternative
    text: 'The printed hic is taken as “this one,” the shepherd, with an implied verb: he will have great
      honor before the Lord. An alternative takes hic as “here,” with the commandment-keepers retaining
      the subject: “and here they will have great honor before the Lord.” The supplied shepherd subject
      remains a contextual interpretation, supported by the honor language in 10.i.3.'
  - marker: c
    reason: textual_variant
    text: The working edition prints et faciunt adversus illum, “and act against him.” Its apparatus reports
      faciunt in Cambridge Dd.IV.11 and its omission in the other Latin manuscripts, with a larger omission
      explained as a jump between similar endings; Palatina and Ethiopic are cited for comparison. This
      is an edition report, not direct collation of that manuscript; the 1856 Cambridge catalogue, entries186–187,
      identifies Dd.IV.11 as the Hermas volume and Dd.IV.12 as a different Jerome volume. That resolves
      the inventory label, not the actual manuscript reading.
lexical_decisions:
- source_word: domine
  chosen: Sir
  alternatives:
  - Lord
  - Master
  rationale: Respectful vocative to the visionary interlocutor; divine Dominum remains Lord.
- source_word: paenitentia
  chosen: repentance
  alternatives:
  - penance
  - change of mind
  rationale: Context concerns moral return after sins; no later penitential institution is inserted.
- source_word: et hic apud Dominum magnum honorem
  chosen: and he will have great honor before the Lord
  alternatives:
  - and here they will have great honor before the Lord
  rationale: Read hic as the shepherd, in continuity with 10.i.3; preserve the alternative adverbial construction
    in footnote.
- source_word: reus fit sanguinis sui / remedium peccatorum
  chosen: becomes guilty of their own blood / a remedy for sins
  alternatives:
  - is responsible for their own death / a cure for sins
  rationale: Keep the blood-guilt and healing language; do not replace remedy by an unexpressed legal
    acquittal.
